title: Iron sent down
hookLine: We sent down iron with great strength and many uses (57:25)

lines: A BRIDGE, A BED, A SWORD.
cards: Look around the room you're in. The nails in the walls. The hinges on the door.

The frame of the chair, the spring in the pen, the steel inside the concrete. A kitchen knife, a hospital bed, a bridge, a sword. A great deal of modern life runs on iron, for building and for breaking.
Surah fifty-seven is named Al-Hadid, the Iron, after one verse near its end, and that verse puts iron in surprising company: right beside scripture and the scales of justice.

teach.h: THE BOOK, THE BALANCE, THE IRON.
teach.b: Verse twenty-five, in paraphrase. God sent his messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance, so that people would stand up for justice.

And God sent down iron, in which there is great strength and many benefits for people, and so that God may know who helps him and his messengers, unseen. Three things in one verse. The Book: guidance, what's right.
The Balance: the mizan from Ar-Rahman, fairness, justice. And iron: power, the means to build, protect and defend. Commentators read them as a set.
Guidance tells you what is just. The balance measures it.
And iron is the strength that can protect justice or crush it.
The striking part is the verb: anzalna, we sent down, the same verb used for the Qur'an itself. What does it mean to send down iron?
Classical commentators pointed to Surah Az-Zumar, where God is said to have sent down cattle for people, eight kinds. There, sent down means created and provided as a gift from above.
Some modern readers connect the verse to astronomy and the idea that iron came to the earth from beyond it. Others are cautious about reading science into a verse.
Either way, the verse says something plain about strength: it's a trust. Iron has great power and many uses, and the same verse asks who will use it to help. The test isn't whether you have strength.
It's which side of the balance you put it on.

how: Muslims read 57:25 as a summary of the messengers' mission: guidance, justice, and the strength to uphold it; the surah takes its name, Al-Hadid, from this verse.

o: a sword carried by the Prophet in battle
the Iron, sent down with great strength
the gold and silver of a rich man's treasury

games.q: three things sent down — tap the pairs.

s: it puts iron beside the Book and the Balance.
the Qur'an also says God 'sent down' cattle
Surah Az-Zumar uses the same verb for eight kinds of cattle.
all commentators agree the verse is about meteorites

games.q: the verse has named the Book, the Balance and iron. what reason does it give for the iron?
o: great strength, many benefits, and to know who helps God and his messengers.
games.why: iron has great strength and many uses, and the verse ties it to who will help, unseen: strength as a test of where it's used.

practice: Hold something made of iron or steel, a key, a spoon, a door handle, and feel its weight, its coolness, how it doesn't bend.
Then think of one strength you have, a skill, a position, a voice others listen to, and ask the verse's question of it: what is this strength helping?

wordCard.voice: Al-Hadid: the iron that Surah Al-Hadid places beside the Book and the Balance, with great strength and many uses, sent down as a trust. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and We sent down iron. anzalna is the same verb used for sending down the Book.
